Inversion In Arbelos

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This picture shows a chain of circles tucked into the gap between two circles that touch.
How to play: Drag the dots O, R, A and B, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Choose how many circles to show, then tick the box to see the guide lines.
Look for the math

Move the points and the chain changes shape. Yet for every circle, however big the gap is, its height above the line is twice its number times its radius. Why should that stay true?

Turning the picture inside out

The two circles touch at O. An inversion centred at O sends them to two straight, parallel lines. The applet puts those lines at A and B. A circle of the chain is tangent to both circles, so its image is tangent to both lines: the images are equal circles, one diameter apart. Circle 0 has its image sitting on the line; circle n has its image n diameters above it.

The height of every circle

Equal circles stacked one diameter apart have height h' = 2n R'. Each original circle and its image are scaled copies from the same centre O, so the ratio of height to radius is the same in both pictures. Hence

hn = 2n Rn

This is the Pappus chain theorem. The logic test checks it for circles 0 to 49 at dozens of settings of O, R, A and B, and again at 300 random drags; it also checks that each circle is really tangent to both given circles and to its neighbours.

Radii, and the ratio k

Let the smaller of the two given circles have radius RL, the larger R, and put k = RR/RL where RR = R − RL. The article gives RL = R/(1+k) and RR = Rk/(1+k), and for the chain

Rn = Rk/(k²n² + k + 1)  and  APn = R(k+2)/(k²n² + k + 1)

With t = 1/k the first formula becomes Rn = Rt/(t² + t + n²). All four formulas are checked over the whole 1–50 range in every test configuration. The applet's own GetCircle builds the equal circles of radius (B−A)/2 spaced B−A apart and inverts them; the second transcription in the test agrees with the core at every circle of every configuration.

About the original

The Java applet used a number spinner from 1 to 50 and a checkbox called "Center lines and common tangents", disabled when only one circle was shown; this page keeps both, with a modern number field and buttons. We follow the article's chain: circle 0 has its diameter on the axis, circle 1 is the next one, and so on. The dashed circles and lines here are the inverted picture the proof uses, not another game to win.

Set the circles to about 5, tick the guide lines, then drag A toward B. Watch the heights change while hn/Rn stays equal to 2n.
